messages.subject: Re: Distance sampling and edge effects
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I had a long email exchange with Eric off-list, which was very helpful. First to copy and paste a sightly more detailed explanation of my sampling plan.

"An example might be 100 independently located 50m transects running perpendicular from the edge directly into the forest. We might expect species A to be an edge specialist, and thus more common in the first 10m where conditions are slightly different, than deeper into the interior. In this instance, I had planned to use classical distance sampling to find the detection probability across all of the data. I would then divide my data into 5 regions; the first regions being observations made across all transects from the edge to 10m. The second would be all observations made between 10m to 20m into the forest, and so on etc."

For the benefit of the distance community, here are a few of the options for tackling the problem described above.

A few useful comments:

1. Read through Miller et al. (2013) in Methods in Ecology and Evolution http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.12105/abstract   The extended example available in an appendix to that paper looks at spotted dolphins in the Gulf of Mexico, but if you substitute "depth" with "distance from forest edge" in that analysis, I think that might take you where you want to go.

2.  Using the model-based approach you can use the results of the modelling that you perform to make inference about the importance of distance from edge for your species of interest.

After adjusting for imperfect detectability, you fit something like a GLM with the appropriate error distribution:

adjusted count = fn(distance-edge, soil-substrate, vegetation-type, ...)

you then make inference about the "distance-edge" coefficients, without using the model to produce abundance estimates.

OR

3. Employing the design-based approach, you can also make progress, but I might take a different approach.  IF (you'll need to assess the veracity of this) you can assume animal density does not vary in the intervals 0-10, 10-20, 20-30, ..., then design your sampling to estimate density in these bands (call them strata if you like).
With your "strata" defined, you can then lay sampling effort randomly into those strata (as I have shown with a zig-zag design).  Program distance can then produce stratum-specific density estimates that you can contrast to assess the veracity of your hypothesis.

4. Eric also pointed out, that rather than make individual DISTANCE projects and analyses for each species, I can build them into a single project "with an additional field in the "observation" layer) as "Species".  Your analysis can then include "filters" whereby you select a specific species for which to fit a detection function and produce a density estimate.  This is a convenience for data management in that the survey information (how many transects, how long, ...) are the same for all species; so you need not duplicate information across multiple distance projects.  In addition, all species are kept in a single file so you need not litter your computer with multiple files."

Particular thanks to Eric for answering many other questions, if anyone has a similar question and wants to find out what our data looked like in due course, feel free to drop my a line on j.s.b...@qmul.ac.uk.

James

On Friday, 17 July 2015 16:20:46 UTC+1, James Borrell wrote:
>
>
> Dear all,
>
> I am planning a study looking at the influence of forest edges on amphibian and reptiles. I was hoping for some advice on how to design the distance analysis.
>
> We would like to produce density estimates for different sections along multiple transect lines e.g. 0-10m, 10-20m, 20-30m
>
> So far, it looks like the best way to do this is to use the sections as a discrete covariate. This produces a single detection probability, and then prints the density for each section.
>
> I appreciate there are some pseudoreplication issues with then comparing the values for the different sections, but it will indicate the distribution of each species with reference to the edge.
>
> I'm very new to distance, does that sound reasonable?
>
> Many thanks,
>
> James
>
>

messages.body_plain:
Ok I'm new to this forum.  I've tried searching for my issue and found related questions, but none of the threads seem to help.

Very simple. I've only ever used Distance to analyze existing survey data.  Now I'm trying to create a survey design.  I have a shapefile with a single polygon that I have added a LinkID field to.  The projection is Projected Coordinate System: NAD_1983_UTM_Zone_11N, Transverse_Mercator,False_Easting 500000.00000000 False_Northing: 0.00000000 Central_Meridian:-117.00000000 Scale_Factor:0.99960000 Latitude_Of_Origin: 0.00000000 Linear Unit: Meter

I matched the default projection for the project to the above (see below)

It is a large survey area 662051 acres.  It displays ok in the Map View, when I move my cursor, the coordinates are correct.  The map tips does not seem to work for it though so perhaps something is wrong.

When I go to create a coverage, no matter what distance I select, I get the initial message telling me that it will generate X number of points and may take a long time and then every time (even if I try a grid spacing of 100m which is ridiculous) I get the error

"No grid points fell inside the survey area.  You should probably try a smaller grid spacing next time"

Nothing gets created

I have created a new project, re-exported the shapefile from the original, double checked that my parameters are ok even tried to use a different projection, but I cannot get this to work.  I am sure it is something very simple, but I'll be darned if I can figure it out.

Here are the Project Geographic Properties:
Geographic Coordinate System "North American 1983"
Projection of Shapefile Data "Transverse Mercator" Parameters: False Easting 500000, False Northing 0, Central Meridian -117, Scale Factor 0.9996 Latitude of Origin 0
Shapefile Units  "Meter"

Maps and Geographic Calculations:
Geographic Coordinate System "North American 1983"
Projection of Shapefile Data "Transverse Mercator" Parameters: False Easting 500000, False Northing 0, Central Meridian -117, Scale Factor 0.9996 Latitude of Origin 0
Map Units  "Meter"

Someone enlighten me please I feel really foolish that I cannot accomplish this simple task.  Even if its just a link to another thread, I would really appreciate it.

Thanks
Marguerite

messages.body_plain:
> Hi Margueritre

I had several issues also trying to import defined areas from shapefiles created outside DISTANCE.

I´ve found a workaround. At the end  copy and paste the vertex of the study area created oustide Distance into the study area.

The steps I use (maybe there are other shortcuts) are:

Create your study area in a GIS
Ita has  to be projected, no matter which projection as at the end you will work with meters or km.
Once you have the Polygons, create from the polygons a feature of points which are in turn the vertex of the Polygon/s
On this point features create columns wich in turn are filled with x and y locations of each vertex
Export them as text file, open and copy them to clipboard.

(Take care of shapes like islands or lakes, they need separators that defines closed areas or "hollows")

Then go to Distance
Create a Study Area without a Coordinate System.
The go to the Data Tab, select the Study Area, at the right you see the Contents of the Layer, double click on the word "Polygon" and a window opens offering to you to possibility to paste all the vertexs from the clipboard.

And then voilá. You have your survey area created, and you may map and create a coverage.

Take care that the last lone in the vertes text file is not without data, because otherwise for some reason your map of the survey area will show very small, as if DISTANCE was doing a far away zoom

If this happens go again, double click the Polygon and will see at the bottom an "separator" that needs to be deleted

This is purely empirical, but  hope this helps.

messages.subject: Small Field Issue
messages.body_plain:
Hi Group,

I’ve taken on a research project comparing grassland bird densities among three different grazing strategies.  Each treatment has 4 reps (pastures).  Pastures were selected based on availability and degree to which they are representative of typical area pastures.  Around here that means they are relatively small (8 – 10.5 ha) and usually irregularly shaped.  Originally, the idea was to use point counts, but an adequate number of non-overlapping points did not fit in many of the pastures, so the decision was made to use line transects.  Lines are parallel, run from pasture edge to edge, vary in length, are oriented to be perpendicular to habitat edges, and were placed randomly.  Minus sampling was necessary due to the area beyond pasture boundaries being either inaccessible or part of another field also in the study.

Due to the size and shape of the pastures, I’m in a situation similar to Fig. 6.6 on pg. 215 in Buckland et al. (2001), except my most extreme pasture has only 3 transects, with both the first and last overlapping the boundary for the majority of their length.  While I’m aware that the technique is robust to having a certain amount of the area of surveyed strips fall outside the boundary, I believe my proportion is substantial.  So, my question…finally…can anyone please point me to a reference explaining a technique for using GIS to determine the proportion of area that is available to be surveyed as a function of distance from the line e(y), as outlined in section 6.7 pg. 215-216 of Buckland et al. (2001)?  Does this need to be done outside Distance software or can I import my pasture and line .shp files into Distance?

All assistance is appreciated!

Kyle Brazil

messages.body_plain:
Kyle:

You raise several issues with regard to placing sampling effort into small strata.  You mentioned rejecting point transects because of overlapping effort.  I recognise you have moved beyond this, but have a look at the simulation study presented in Buckland (2006) Point transect surveys for songbirds: robust methodologies <https://risweb.st-andrews.ac.uk:443/portal/en/researchoutput/point-transect-surveys-for-songbirds-robust-methodologies%2881994469-4da3-4920-b642-428161e84c47%29.html> The Auk. 123(2):345-357.  Have a look at results in Table 5 showing minimal bias (0.56%) for severe overlap between point count stations.

But to your specific question about how to compute e(y) using GIS; this cannot be done inside Distance and must be undertaken with GIS software outside of Distance.  The Auk simulation study discusses this edge effect also, you might gain some insights into the calculation of e(y) (in the context of point transects) from that paper.
